title: Refresh cycles fused with page fingerprinting for in-DRAM dedup
idea: Combine the mandatory refresh operation with content hashing: a tiny CRC/hash unit at each subarray's sense amplifiers folds every row into a 32-bit signature as it is refreshed and writes it to a reserved signature row. The controller reads the signature table every 64 ms, verifies candidate matches and merges duplicate pages by remapping, replacing CPU-driven KSM scanning.
why: Dedup recovers 10-40% of capacity on VM/container hosts but today costs CPU and bandwidth to scan; piggybacking on refresh (fact 3) makes always-on dedup nearly free, so fewer DRAM bits per host.

title: Confidential-computing integrity MACs reused as dedup fingerprints
idea: Combine the per-line MACs and integrity tree that memory-encryption engines (TDX/SEV-SNP style) already compute with a deduplication index: read-only pages encrypted under a shared convergent 'dedup key domain' produce identical MAC roots, so the controller detects and merges them without decrypting.
why: Encrypted VMs currently make page dedup impossible; this regains 15-30% of host memory in confidential clouds with zero extra hashing hardware.

title: Row-hammer activation counters double as page-hotness telemetry
idea: Combine DDR5 per-row activation counting (PRAC, built for row-hammer defense) with OS memory tiering: expose a decayed counter summary through a mode-register/sideband read so the kernel knows exactly which rows are cold without page-table access-bit scanning, and demotes them to CXL, compressed or flash tiers.
why: Accurate, free hotness data lets 30-50% of resident pages move to cheaper tiers with little slowdown, cutting top-tier DRAM per server by about a third; reuses silicon already paid for (fact 9).

title: Compression-funded inline ECC eliminates the dedicated ECC chips
idea: Combine lossless cache-line compression (base-delta / frequent-pattern) with error correction: any 64 B line that compresses by at least 8 B stores its own strong ECC in the freed bits, so the 9th/10th ECC DRAM device on each server rank is dropped. Rare incompressible lines spill to a small overflow region flagged by a pointer bit.
why: Removes the 12.5-25% of DRAM bits that servers spend on ECC devices while keeping chipkill-class protection.

title: Idle GPU video encoders compress the LLM KV cache
idea: Combine the motion-compensated inter-frame prediction of on-die AV1/HEVC encoders with attention KV tensors: treat each head's K/V across successive token blocks as video frames, encode residuals in the otherwise idle media engine, and decode blocks back into HBM just before attention reads them.
why: KV cache dominates inference memory; temporal and cross-head redundancy could yield 4-8x KV compression using silicon that already sits unused on datacenter GPUs (facts 5, 6).

title: Texture-compression units serve as free neural-weight decompressors
idea: Combine GPU fixed-function texture block decoders (ASTC/BC7 endpoints-plus-indices) with weight storage: quantize weight matrices into 4x4 blocks fitted with learned endpoints, store them as compressed textures, and fetch through the texture path straight into the tensor-core operand feed.
why: 3-5 bits per weight with zero added decode logic or ALU cost, cutting HBM capacity spent on weights 3-5x versus BF16.

title: Learned index replaces the SSD's flash-translation DRAM
idea: Combine learned index structures (piecewise-linear models over sorted keys) with the SSD flash translation layer: because FTL writes are mostly sequential within streams, a few MB of linear segments plus a small exception table map LBAs to flash pages instead of a 4-byte-per-4KB page table held in DRAM.
why: Enterprise SSDs carry ~1 GB of DRAM per TB; a 50-100x smaller map returns a noticeable slice of global DRAM bit demand to host use.

title: Store context as entropy-coded tokens, regenerate KV on demand
idea: Combine the model's own next-token probabilities with arithmetic coding: cold context is evicted from the KV cache and kept only as token IDs coded at ~1-2 bits per token, and when attention needs a span a burst prefill kernel recomputes its K/V. A tiny per-span key summary decides when recompute is worth it.
why: A token's KV is ~50-300 KB in large models versus under one byte as coded text, so long-context DRAM drops by orders of magnitude, paid for with abundant compute.

title: Page-aligned pruning plus copy-on-write zero page
idea: Combine the OS shared zero frame with structured sparsity: train or prune so whole 4-64 KB weight/activation blocks are exactly zero, then map those virtual pages to one physical zero frame; the GPU/CPU MMU flags them so reads return zeros without touching DRAM.
why: 30-60% block-sparse models shrink physically with no new tensor format or kernels, and bandwidth to zero pages disappears too.

title: Bit-plane tensor layout enables precision-on-demand memory
idea: Combine image bit-plane slicing with memory placement: store each BF16/FP8 tensor as separate pages per bit plane (sign+exponent, high mantissa, low mantissa). Low-significance planes are placed in compressed or slower tiers or dropped under pressure, and kernels fetch only the planes their current precision needs.
why: 25-50% of tensor bytes become optional, so memory pressure degrades precision gracefully instead of forcing OOM or swap.

title: Garbage collector fused with a columnar compressor for old generation
idea: Combine the generational GC's copying/promotion phase with compression: objects promoted to the old generation are packed into per-class columnar blocks (field-transposed, delta- and dictionary-encoded), and a read barrier decompresses on access through a small decoded-object cache.
why: Managed heaps (Java, Go, JS, Python) run at 2-5x live data with highly redundant fields; a 2-3x old-gen shrink is plausible.

title: Erasure coding replaces triple replication in in-memory stores
idea: Combine storage-style Reed-Solomon coding with in-memory data grids (Redis, parameter servers, session stores): keep k data shards plus m parity shards across nodes and update parity with RDMA-shipped XOR deltas on writes instead of holding three full DRAM replicas.
why: Replica memory falls from 3x to ~1.5x for the same failure tolerance.

title: Hashed compositional embeddings plus a learned head cache
idea: Combine the hashing trick (each ID composes its vector from several shared sub-tables via independent hashes) with a small table of fully learned rows for the hottest IDs; IDs are promoted to full rows as their frequency rises and demoted when they cool.
why: Recommendation models hold multi-TB embedding tables in DRAM; the long tail compresses 10-50x with little accuracy loss.

title: Tidal memory: scheduler pairs anti-correlated job footprints
idea: Combine the cluster scheduler with per-job memory-phase profiles: co-locate jobs whose peak footprints alternate in time (nightly ETL vs daytime serving, train vs eval phases) and shuttle the idle job's pages to a CXL/compressed tier at each phase boundary.
why: Servers are provisioned for each job's peak; sharing peaks across time cuts installed DRAM 25-40% fleet-wide.

title: JIT profiler narrows object fields with deoptimizing guards
idea: Combine JIT profiling with value-range compression: the runtime observes that fields only hold small ranges (counters under 65k, few enum values, pointers within one region) and rewrites class layouts to 16-, 8- or 2-bit fields, falling back to wide layouts when a guard catches an overflow.
why: Object-heavy services could shrink heaps 30-50% with no source changes.

title: Error-bounded scientific compression built into the memory controller
idea: Combine ZFP/SZ-style transform coding with the memory controller: pages tagged approximate-OK (simulation fields, activations, gradients) are stored at fixed rates of 8-16 bits per float with guaranteed absolute error bounds, using fixed-rate blocks so random access stays O(1).
why: 2-4x capacity for floating-point working sets that tolerate bounded error.

title: Vector-database index fused with the attention KV cache
idea: Combine an approximate-nearest-neighbor index (IVF/HNSW over key vectors) with the KV cache: only centroids and the graph stay in DRAM, full K/V live in flash or a CXL tier, and each decode step retrieves just the top-k tokens with the highest query-key scores.
why: 10-20x less DRAM for million-token contexts, because attention mass concentrates on few tokens.

title: Vision token-merging applied to KV cache compaction
idea: Combine ViT bipartite token merging with KV eviction: adjacent tokens whose keys are highly similar merge into a weighted centroid K/V with a stored count, and attention adds log(count) to the logit so merged entries keep their probability mass.
why: 2-4x KV reduction with lower quality loss than hard eviction.

title: Copy-on-write base pages plus sparse deltas for full fine-tunes
idea: Combine page-level copy-on-write sharing with delta compression of fully fine-tuned models: each variant is stored as the base model's pages plus sparse, quantized delta pages, and the GPU load path composes base+delta tile by tile into SRAM during GEMM.
why: Serving 50 full fine-tunes costs about one base plus 50 small deltas (each ~5-10% of base) instead of 50 full copies.

title: RAID-5 parity across DIMMs replaces per-rank chipkill
idea: Combine RAID-5 striping with main memory: one parity DIMM covers a group of 4-8 data DIMMs, a per-line CRC carried in burst metadata detects errors, and reconstruction from parity runs only when a CRC fails, replacing per-rank ECC devices.
why: Reliability overhead drops from 12.5-25% of bits to ~6-12% at similar device-failure tolerance.

title: Switch multicast streams one shared weight copy to all GPUs
idea: Combine a pooled weight store (CXL/NVLink memory node) with switch-level multicast: data-parallel replicas run in lockstep and the switch broadcasts each layer's weights just in time to every GPU, which keeps only a two-layer ring buffer instead of a full replica in HBM.
why: HBM spent on duplicated weights falls by the replica count (8-64x), freeing it for KV cache or allowing smaller-HBM parts (fact 6).

title: Segment-base hardware makes 32-bit compressed pointers universal
idea: Combine x86-style segment base registers with pointer compression: the load/store unit adds a per-region base plus a 3-bit shift to 32-bit references in a single cycle, so C/C++/Rust allocators and runtimes can use compressed pointers in any heap, not only JVM/V8-style ones.
why: Pointer-heavy structures (graphs, trees, ASTs, indexes) shrink 30-40%.

title: Router lookahead predicts MoE experts for just-in-time paging
idea: Combine the mixture-of-experts gating network with a prefetcher: a cheap distilled copy of layer L+2's router runs on layer L's hidden state to predict which experts will fire, and those experts are paged from flash/CXL into HBM two layers ahead, so only ~10-20% of experts are resident.
why: MoE models leave 80-95% of weights inactive per token; DRAM for weights shrinks 5-10x.

title: DIMM data-buffer chip doubles as a base-delta decompressor
idea: Combine the MRDIMM/LRDIMM data-buffer and RCD chips (already made on 28-40 nm DUV processes) with a base-delta-immediate compression engine and a small remap table, so a DIMM built from older 1y/1z DUV DRAM dies presents ~1.6-2x its raw capacity to the host.
why: Lets non-EUV DRAM nodes match EUV-node logical density per module, skipping the 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4) while all added logic stays on mature, U.S.-available nodes.

title: Log-structured SLC NAND tier with DRAM as write absorber
idea: Combine log-structured file-system writes with a CXL memory device built from SLC 3D NAND (DUV-made) plus a small DRAM buffer: evicted dirty pages are appended sequentially into erase blocks, DRAM holds the hot set and log head, and a 28 nm controller cleans segments during idle time so random writes never hit NAND directly.
why: NAND is roughly 1/10 the cost per bit and needs no EUV; moving the cold 60-70% of memory onto it cuts DRAM per server 2-3x while respecting endurance.

title: TSV-stacked read-optimized NAND beside the accelerator for weights
idea: Combine HBM-style TSV stacking and wide I/O on a mature-node base die with NAND dies tuned for massive read parallelism, dedicated to read-only inference weights; the accelerator's HBM keeps only KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are read-only so NAND endurance is irrelevant; 8-16x capacity per stack versus HBM DRAM, with no EUV layer in either the NAND or the base die.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM stores frozen foundation-model weights
idea: Combine core-rope / mask-ROM hard-wiring with LLM deployment: a frozen base model's quantized weights are encoded in one via layer of a 40-65 nm DUV logic process (one transistor or less per bit, multi-level via codes) next to the compute array, while only LoRA adapters and KV use writable DRAM.
why: Removes weights from DRAM entirely for stable models using only mature DUV processes; only the via mask changes per model, so NRE stays low.

title: Fiber delay-line carousel circulates weights past pipelined accelerators
idea: Combine 1950s delay-line memory with WDM optics: model weights circulate continuously in a 10-20 km amplified fiber loop at ~25 Tb/s aggregate, and each pipeline-stage accelerator taps the wavelengths carrying its layer exactly when they pass, so weights are stored in flight instead of in DRAM.
why: Holds ~150-300 MB per loop with zero lithography; fits strictly sequential weight streaming, though the ~50-100 us lap latency rules out random access.

title: Retired DDR4 DIMMs pooled behind a compressing CXL controller
idea: Combine decommissioned DDR4 modules (built on pre-EUV nodes) with a 28 nm CXL pooling controller that adds inline compression and per-DIMM health remapping, deployed as the far-memory tier of new servers instead of being shredded.
why: Adds usable supply from bits that already exist with no fab; compression offsets lower density, and recyclers or OEMs can run it as a takeback business.

title: Retired GPUs become attention-computing KV-cache servers
idea: Combine previous-generation accelerators (HBM2-era parts on non-EUV processes) with attention offload: the new GPU ships query vectors over the network, the retired GPU holds long-context KV in its HBM and returns attention outputs, so only small vectors cross the link.
why: Turns stranded HBM2 into extra KV capacity without new DRAM and frees 50-70% of new GPUs' HBM for weights and batch.

title: DRAM and NAND dies in one stack with self-tiering base die
idea: Combine a few older-node DRAM dies and several NAND dies in one bonded/TSV stack over a 28 nm logic base die that tracks page heat and migrates 4 KB pages between DRAM and NAND internally at TSV bandwidth, presenting one flat byte-addressable space.
why: Gives ~4-8x capacity per package from mostly DUV NAND bits; in-package migration avoids host-side tiering overhead and channel traffic.

title: Mature-node fat capacitors enable tri-level DRAM for approximate data
idea: Combine NAND-style multi-level sensing with DRAM on a relaxed DUV node, where larger cells hold enough charge for three levels: a two-step sense amplifier resolves 0/half/1, storing 1.58 bits per cell for error-tolerant data such as activations, low mantissa planes or KV, with a binary mode for everything else.
why: +58% bits per cell without lithographic shrink, turning the absence of EUV (bigger cells, more charge, fact 1) into multi-level margin.

title: NOR flash analog arrays compute FFN layers in place
idea: Combine 40 nm embedded NOR flash cells with analog matrix-vector multiplication: transformer feed-forward weights (~2/3 of parameters) are programmed as cell conductances and compute in place, while attention and KV stay digital in a small DRAM.
why: FFN weights never occupy DRAM; 40-55 nm NOR is DUV-only and domestically fabbable, though accuracy is limited by analog noise and drift.

title: Mainframe-style page-only DRAM die strips column periphery
idea: Combine IBM's expanded-storage concept (page-addressable-only memory) with a DRAM die redesign: a die accessed only in 4 KB blocks drops fine column decoders, most data-path muxing and per-bank DLL logic, giving much of the ~49% periphery area back to cells on a DUV node; it serves as the tier below byte-addressable DRAM.
why: ~1.4-1.7x bits per mm2 on non-EUV nodes (fact 7) at the cost of block access; main DRAM shrinks because cold pages live here.

title: CXL switch holds a rack-wide page dedup table
idea: Combine the CXL switch's address-routing tables (mature-node switch silicon) with a global content-hash index: identical pages across every host in a rack (OS images, runtimes, model weights) are stored once in pooled memory and mapped read-only into each host, with copy-on-write on modification.
why: Cross-host duplication in a rack far exceeds per-host duplication, so 20-40% of pooled capacity could be saved.

title: Fleet-trained shared dictionaries for memory page compression
idea: Combine zstd-style trained dictionaries with a mature-node CXL memory-compression controller: the operator trains dictionaries offline on sampled page contents per workload class, loads them into controller SRAM, and tags each compressed page with its dictionary ID.
why: Shared dictionaries roughly double ratios on small 4 KB pages (about 2x to 3-4x), so a mature-node controller over older DRAM delivers more effective capacity than raw EUV parts.

title: Drum-era optimum placement lays out weights for flash streaming
idea: Combine 1950s drum 'optimum programming' (placing data where the head will be when needed) with LLM inference from NVMe: the compiler stripes each layer's weights across all NAND channels, dies and planes in exact consumption order and double-buffers into DRAM overlays of a fixed budget so flash reads fully overlap compute.
why: Ordinary DUV-made SSDs stream weights at full internal bandwidth, so DRAM shrinks to a few layers' worth (10-50x less for batch inference).

title: Reversible layers fused with backprop eliminate activation storage
idea: Combine reversible (bijective) residual blocks with training: activations are reconstructed exactly from layer outputs during the backward pass instead of being stored, using fixed-point coupling functions so reconstruction never drifts.
why: Activation memory, often the largest training footprint, becomes constant in depth, cutting training DRAM/HBM 3-10x on any hardware including mature-node accelerators.

title: Succinct filters plus on-flash learned index shrink key-value indexes
idea: Combine ribbon/cuckoo filters with a learned on-flash index: a DRAM-resident filter (~1 byte per key) answers whether a key exists and in which segment, and a learned model stored on the SSD locates the record in one read, replacing full in-DRAM hash indexes.
why: Index DRAM falls from ~16-40 bytes per key to ~1-2 bytes per key for billion-key stores, using only commodity DUV-made SSDs.

title: Partial-good DRAM dies salvaged via controller remap
idea: Combine wafer-sort binning with controller-side sparing: DUV-node DRAM dies that fail spec in a few banks or subarrays (normally scrapped) are sold as reduced-capacity parts with a fuse map that the memory controller reads at boot to remap around bad regions.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer by several percent with no new tools, which matters when every non-EUV wafer counts.

title: Real-time memory exchange fused with VM balloon drivers
idea: Combine spot-market pricing with hypervisor ballooning: tenants post idle guest memory as sell orders, the balloon driver reclaims it within seconds when bought, and the buyer receives it through a CXL pool or same-host remapping.
why: Cloud memory utilization often sits under 50%; trading idle gigabytes raises effective supply 20-30% with no new silicon.

title: Discounted compressed-memory instance tier sold to tenants
idea: Combine cloud billing with transparent zswap/controller compression: sell instances priced per logical GB at a discount where the provider backs part of the memory with compressed pages, and expose per-tenant compression stats so customers restructure data to compress better.
why: Aligns price signals with compressibility; a 1.5-2x fleet effective-capacity gain means fewer DRAM bits purchased.

title: SmartNIC fuses page compression with far-memory transport
idea: Combine a 28 nm FPGA SmartNIC's packet pipeline with a page compressor: pages evicted to remote memory are compressed, encrypted and RDMA-sent in one pass, and on fault the NIC decompresses directly into the host page, so far memory costs no CPU and stores 2-3x more per remote GB.
why: Makes rack-level far memory over commodity Ethernet practical, so each server needs less local DRAM.

title: Datacenter-wide prompt-prefix KV cache on flash servers
idea: Combine content-addressed storage with LLM prefill: KV blocks for common prefixes (system prompts, documents, tool schemas) are hashed by token sequence and stored once on NAND-heavy cache servers, and inference GPUs fetch matching prefix blocks over RDMA instead of recomputing them or pinning them in HBM.
why: Deduplicates the large share of KV repeated across users, cutting per-GPU KV footprint and prefill compute, built entirely from DUV-made NAND and mature networking.

title: Memory-footprint budgets written into federal software procurement
idea: Combine the software bill of materials (SBOM) requirement with a measured memory-footprint disclosure: federally procured software must report peak and steady-state RSS on standardized workloads, and contracts score bids on GB per transaction.
why: Shifts demand: a 20-30% cut in software bloat across government and contractors frees DRAM supply without fabs, and the disclosure norm spreads to industry.

title: 28 nm SRAM-chain pipeline with codebook weights replaces DRAM
idea: Combine weight-stationary pipeline parallelism across many 28 nm SRAM-rich chips (~300 MB each) with 2-3-bit vector-quantized codebook weights decoded at the MAC array, so a whole model lives in mature-node SRAM spread along a board-level chain.
why: Eliminates DRAM for inference with all-DUV, U.S.-fabbable silicon, trading more die area for zero EUV, zero DRAM and very high bandwidth.
